description: Exponential and trigonometric integrals, Fresnel and error-function relatives, additional orthogonal polynomials, zeta-type functions, regularized gamma and beta functions, generalized hypergeometric and Meijer G functions, spherical and cylindrical Bessel relatives, elliptic and Mathieu functions, piecewise and periodic waveform functions, angular-momentum coefficients and the remaining elementary functions.

tools.name: ExpIntegralEi
tools.description: The exponential integral Ei(z) = -PV Integral of Exp[-t]/t from -z to infinity; ExpIntegralE[n, z] is the generalized exponential integral E_n(z) used in radiative transfer and Laplace-transform tables. Both are analytic in the cut plane and evaluate to arbitrary precision.
tools.usage:
ExpIntegralEi[z]
ExpIntegralE[n, z]
tools.example:
Integrate[Exp[t]/t, t] (* ExpIntegralEi[t] *)
N[ExpIntegralE[2, 1.5], 20]

tools.name: LogIntegral
tools.description: The logarithmic integral li(z) = Integral of 1/Log[t] from 0 to z, the classical approximation to the prime-counting function PrimePi. Also appears in Riemann's explicit formulas together with ZetaZero.
tools.usage: LogIntegral[z]

tools.name: SinIntegral
tools.description: Sine integral Si(z) = Integral of Sin[t]/t from 0 to z; CosIntegral, SinhIntegral and CoshIntegral are the companions. They arise in Fourier analysis (Gibbs phenomenon), antenna theory and the integral of Sinc.
tools.usage:
SinIntegral[z]
CosIntegral[z]
SinhIntegral[z]
CoshIntegral[z]
tools.example:
Integrate[Sin[t]/t, {t, 0, x}] (* SinIntegral[x] *)
Limit[SinIntegral[x], x -> Infinity] (* Pi/2 *)

tools.name: FresnelS
tools.description: Fresnel integrals S(z) and C(z) (integrals of Sin[Pi t^2/2] and Cos[Pi t^2/2]), used in near-field diffraction, Cornu spirals and road/rail clothoid transition curves. FresnelF and FresnelG give the auxiliary functions.
tools.usage:
FresnelS[z]
FresnelC[z]
FresnelF[z]
FresnelG[z]
tools.example:
ParametricPlot[{FresnelC[t], FresnelS[t]}, {t, -5, 5}] (* Cornu spiral *)
Limit[FresnelS[x], x -> Infinity] (* 1/2 *)

tools.name: InverseErf
tools.description: Inverse error function (InverseErfc for the complementary one), needed to compute normal quantiles and confidence bounds symbolically; Erfi[z] = -I Erf[I z] is the imaginary error function and DawsonF the Dawson integral.
tools.usage:
InverseErf[s]
InverseErfc[s]
Erfi[z]
DawsonF[z]

parameters.name: s
parameters.description: Value in (-1, 1) for InverseErf, (0, 2) for InverseErfc.

tools.example:
Sqrt[2] InverseErf[2 0.975 - 1] (* 1.95996: 97.5% normal quantile *)
InverseCDF[NormalDistribution[], p] (* Symbolic form uses InverseErfc *)

tools.name: GammaRegularized
tools.description: Regularized incomplete gamma function Q(a, z) = Gamma[a, z]/Gamma[a] (with a two-limit form), and InverseGammaRegularized for its inverse; BetaRegularized I_z(a, b) and InverseBetaRegularized are the beta analogues. They give the CDFs of the gamma, chi-squared, Poisson, beta, binomial, t and F distributions in closed form.
tools.usage:
GammaRegularized[a, z]
GammaRegularized[a, z0, z1]
InverseGammaRegularized[a, s]
BetaRegularized[z, a, b]
InverseBetaRegularized[s, a, b]
tools.example:
CDF[ChiSquareDistribution[4], x] (* GammaRegularized[2, 0, x/2] *)
BetaRegularized[0.5, 2, 3]
InverseGammaRegularized[3, 0.05]

tools.name: GegenbauerC
tools.description: Gegenbauer (ultraspherical) polynomials C_n^(lambda)(x); JacobiP[n, a, b, x] are the Jacobi polynomials that generalize Legendre, Chebyshev and Gegenbauer, ChebyshevU the Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind, LegendreQ the Legendre functions of the second kind and ZernikeR the Zernike radial polynomials used in optics. All are orthogonal-polynomial families for spectral methods.
tools.usage:
GegenbauerC[n, lambda, x]
JacobiP[n, a, b, x]
ChebyshevU[n, x]
LegendreQ[n, x]
ZernikeR[n, m, r]
tools.example:
GegenbauerC[3, 1/2, x] == LegendreP[3, x] // Simplify
JacobiP[2, 1, 1, x] // Expand
Integrate[ChebyshevU[2, x] ChebyshevU[3, x] Sqrt[1 - x^2], {x, -1, 1}] (* 0: orthogonality *)

tools.name: HurwitzZeta
tools.description: Hurwitz zeta function zeta(s, a) = Sum 1/(k + a)^s, generalizing Zeta; LerchPhi[z, s, a] is the Lerch transcendent generalizing both PolyLog and HurwitzZeta, StieltjesGamma[n] the Stieltjes constants in the Laurent expansion of Zeta at 1, and RiemannSiegelZ/RiemannSiegelTheta the functions used to locate zeta zeros on the critical line.
tools.usage:
HurwitzZeta[s, a]
LerchPhi[z, s, a]
StieltjesGamma[n]
RiemannSiegelZ[t]
RiemannSiegelTheta[t]
tools.example:
HurwitzZeta[2, 1] == Zeta[2]
Sum[1/(k + 1/3)^3, {k, 0, Infinity}] (* HurwitzZeta[3, 1/3] *)
Plot[RiemannSiegelZ[t], {t, 0, 50}]

tools.name: HypergeometricPFQ
tools.description: Generalized hypergeometric function pFq({a1, ..., ap}, {b1, ..., bq}, z), the closed form for most sums of ratios of Pochhammer symbols; Hypergeometric0F1 and HypergeometricU (Tricomi confluent) are the common special members. Sum and Integrate frequently return these; FunctionExpand converts them to elementary or classical special functions where possible.
tools.usage:
HypergeometricPFQ[{a1, ..., ap}, {b1, ..., bq}, z]
Hypergeometric0F1[a, z]
HypergeometricU[a, b, z]
HypergeometricPFQRegularized[{a}, {b}, z]
tools.example:
Sum[x^k/(k!)^2, {k, 0, Infinity}] (* Hypergeometric0F1[1, x] = BesselI[0, 2 Sqrt[x]] *)
FunctionExpand[HypergeometricPFQ[{1/2}, {3/2}, -z^2]] (* involves Erf *)

tools.name: MeijerG
tools.description: The Meijer G-function G^{m,n}_{p,q}, the very general special function (with FoxH even more general) in terms of which Wolfram's definite integration and Mellin-transform algorithms express results; MeijerGReduce converts expressions to G-function form. Useful for symbolic integration of products of special functions.
tools.example:
MeijerGReduce[BesselJ[0, x], x]
FunctionExpand[MeijerG[{{}, {}}, {{0}, {}}, z]] (* Exp[-z] *)

tools.name: SphericalHarmonicY
tools.description: Spherical harmonics Y_l^m(theta, phi), the angular eigenfunctions of the Laplacian on the sphere used in quantum mechanics, geodesy, antenna theory and lighting (SH lighting). Normalized so that they are orthonormal over the sphere; SphericalPlot3D visualizes them.
tools.usage: SphericalHarmonicY[l, m, theta, phi]
tools.example:
SphericalHarmonicY[2, 1, theta, phi]
SphericalPlot3D[Abs[SphericalHarmonicY[3, 2, t, p]]^2, {t, 0, Pi}, {p, 0, 2 Pi}]

tools.name: SphericalBesselJ
tools.description: Spherical Bessel functions j_n(z) and y_n(z) (SphericalBesselY), plus SphericalHankelH1/H2, solving the radial part of the Helmholtz equation in spherical coordinates (scattering, acoustics, quantum wells). HankelH1/HankelH2 are the ordinary cylindrical Hankel functions, and BesselJZero/BesselYZero give the zeros needed for eigenvalue problems.
tools.usage:
SphericalBesselJ[n, z]
SphericalBesselY[n, z]
SphericalHankelH1[n, z]
HankelH1[nu, z]
HankelH2[nu, z]
BesselJZero[nu, k]
BesselYZero[nu, k]
tools.example:
SphericalBesselJ[1, z] // FunctionExpand (* Sin[z]/z^2 - Cos[z]/z *)
N[BesselJZero[0, 3]] (* 8.65373 *)
Table[BesselJZero[0, k], {k, 3}] // N (* drum-head eigenvalues *)

tools.name: AiryBi
tools.description: Airy function of the second kind Bi(z), with AiryAiPrime and AiryBiPrime the derivatives and AiryAiZero/AiryBiZero the zeros; together with AiryAi they solve y'' = z y (turning points in WKB, quantum triangular wells, optics caustics).
tools.usage:
AiryBi[z]
AiryAiPrime[z]
AiryBiPrime[z]
AiryAiZero[k]
AiryBiZero[k]
tools.example:
DSolve[y''[x] == x y[x], y, x] (* C1 AiryAi[x] + C2 AiryBi[x] *)
N[AiryAiZero[1]] (* -2.33811 *)

tools.name: StruveH
tools.description: Struve functions H_nu(z) and L_nu(z) (StruveL), particular solutions of the inhomogeneous Bessel equation appearing in acoustic radiation impedance and electromagnetic diffraction; KelvinBer/Bei/Ker/Kei are the Kelvin functions used for skin-effect in conductors.
tools.usage:
StruveH[nu, z]
StruveL[nu, z]
KelvinBer[nu, z]
KelvinBei[nu, z]
KelvinKer[nu, z]
KelvinKei[nu, z]
tools.example:
Plot[{StruveH[0, x], BesselY[0, x]}, {x, 0, 20}]
KelvinBer[0, 2.5]

tools.name: WhittakerM
tools.description: Whittaker functions M_{k,m}(z) and W_{k,m}(z) (WhittakerW), the standard solutions of Whittaker's confluent hypergeometric equation; they appear in the hydrogen atom, Coulomb wave functions (CoulombF, CoulombG) and parabolic cylinder problems (ParabolicCylinderD).
tools.usage:
WhittakerM[k, m, z]
WhittakerW[k, m, z]
CoulombF[l, eta, rho]
CoulombG[l, eta, rho]
ParabolicCylinderD[nu, z]
tools.example:
WhittakerM[k, m, z] // FunctionExpand (* in terms of Hypergeometric1F1 *)
ParabolicCylinderD[2, x] // FunctionExpand

tools.name: MathieuC
tools.description: Even and odd Mathieu functions ce and se (MathieuC, MathieuS) with their derivatives (MathieuCPrime, MathieuSPrime) and characteristic values (MathieuCharacteristicA, MathieuCharacteristicB, MathieuCharacteristicExponent); they solve Mathieu's equation y'' + (a - 2 q Cos[2 z]) y = 0 governing elliptic membranes, parametric resonance and ion traps.
tools.usage:
MathieuC[a, q, z]
MathieuS[a, q, z]
MathieuCharacteristicA[r, q]
MathieuCharacteristicB[r, q]
MathieuCharacteristicExponent[a, q]
tools.example:
a2 = MathieuCharacteristicA[2, 1];
Plot[MathieuC[a2, 1, z], {z, 0, 2 Pi}]
(* stability chart of the Mathieu equation *)
RegionPlot[Im[MathieuCharacteristicExponent[a, q]] == 0, {a, -5, 20}, {q, 0, 10}]

tools.name: EllipticF
tools.description: Incomplete elliptic integral of the first kind F(phi | m), with EllipticPi the complete/incomplete third kind and EllipticTheta the Jacobi theta functions; EllipticNomeQ and InverseEllipticNomeQ convert between parameter and nome. Note the parameter convention m = k^2, not the modulus k.
tools.usage:
EllipticF[phi, m]
EllipticPi[n, m]
EllipticPi[n, phi, m]
EllipticTheta[a, u, q]
EllipticNomeQ[m]
tools.example:
Integrate[1/Sqrt[1 - m Sin[t]^2], {t, 0, phi}] (* EllipticF[phi, m] *)
(* pendulum period with amplitude theta0 *)
T = 4 Sqrt[l/g] EllipticK[Sin[theta0/2]^2]

tools.name: JacobiCN
tools.description: Jacobi elliptic functions cn and dn (JacobiCN, JacobiDN; JacobiSN is already listed) with the other nine (JacobiNS, JacobiSC, ...), JacobiAmplitude am(u | m) and the inverses InverseJacobiSN etc. They are the exact solutions of the pendulum, the Duffing oscillator and KdV cnoidal waves.
tools.usage:
JacobiCN[u, m]
JacobiDN[u, m]
JacobiAmplitude[u, m]
InverseJacobiSN[v, m]
InverseJacobiCN[v, m]
tools.example:
JacobiSN[u, m]^2 + JacobiCN[u, m]^2 // Simplify (* 1 *)
(* pendulum: theta[t] = 2 ArcSin[k JacobiSN[t, k^2]] *)
Plot[2 ArcSin[0.9 JacobiSN[t, 0.81]], {t, 0, 20}]

tools.name: DedekindEta
tools.description: Dedekind eta function eta(tau), with KleinInvariantJ the modular j-invariant and ModularLambda the elliptic modular lambda function, all defined on the upper half-plane; together with EllipticTheta they form the modular-form toolkit used in number theory, string theory and lattice sums.
tools.usage:
DedekindEta[tau]
KleinInvariantJ[tau]
ModularLambda[tau]

parameters.name: tau
parameters.description: Complex number with positive imaginary part.

tools.example:
KleinInvariantJ[I] (* 1 *)
N[DedekindEta[I], 20]
ComplexPlot[KleinInvariantJ[z], {z, -1 + 0.05 I, 1 + 1.5 I}]

tools.name: MittagLefflerE
tools.description: Mittag-Leffler function E_alpha(z) and E_{alpha,beta}(z), the generalization of the exponential that solves fractional differential equations (FractionalD / CaputoD) and models anomalous relaxation and viscoelasticity.
tools.usage:
MittagLefflerE[alpha, z]
MittagLefflerE[alpha, beta, z]
tools.example:
MittagLefflerE[1, z] (* Exp[z] *)
Plot[MittagLefflerE[1/2, -t], {t, 0, 5}] (* fractional relaxation *)
DSolve[CaputoD[y[t], {t, 1/2}] == -y[t], y[t], t]
tools.notes: Introduced in 12.3 together with FractionalD and CaputoD.

tools.name: CarlsonRF
tools.description: Carlson symmetric elliptic integrals R_F, R_C, R_D, R_G, R_J (CarlsonRF, CarlsonRC, CarlsonRD, CarlsonRG, CarlsonRJ), the numerically stable symmetric alternative to Legendre's elliptic integrals; every EllipticK/E/F/Pi can be written in terms of them.
tools.usage:
CarlsonRF[x, y, z]
CarlsonRC[x, y]
CarlsonRD[x, y, z]
CarlsonRG[x, y, z]
CarlsonRJ[x, y, z, rho]
tools.example:
CarlsonRF[0, 1 - m, 1] == EllipticK[m] // FullSimplify
N[CarlsonRF[1, 2, 3], 20]

tools.name: HeunG
tools.description: General Heun function HeunG (with confluent forms HeunC, HeunD, HeunB, HeunT and their derivatives HeunGPrime etc.), the solution of the Heun equation with four regular singular points that covers Lame, Mathieu-like and many black-hole perturbation and quantum problems beyond the hypergeometric class. Available since 12.1.
tools.usage:
HeunG[a, q, alpha, beta, gamma, delta, z]
HeunC[q, alpha, gamma, delta, epsilon, z]
HeunGPrime[a, q, alpha, beta, gamma, delta, z]
tools.example:
DSolve[y''[z] + (gamma/z + delta/(z - 1) + (alpha + beta - gamma - delta + 1)/(z - a)) y'[z] + (alpha beta z - q)/(z (z - 1) (z - a)) y[z] == 0, y, z]
N[HeunG[2, 1/2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1/3], 15]

tools.name: AppellF1
tools.description: Appell hypergeometric function F1 of two variables, with AppellF2, AppellF3, AppellF4 (13.x) completing the family; they arise when integrating products of powers of several linear factors (Feynman parameters, elliptic-type integrals). FunctionExpand reduces special cases to 2F1.
tools.usage:
AppellF1[a, b1, b2, c, x, y]
AppellF2[a, b1, b2, c1, c2, x, y]
tools.example:
Integrate[t^(a - 1) (1 - t)^(c - a - 1) (1 - x t)^(-b1) (1 - y t)^(-b2), {t, 0, 1}, Assumptions -> 0 < a < c && 0 < x < 1 && 0 < y < 1]
(* Gamma[a] Gamma[c - a]/Gamma[c] AppellF1[a, b1, b2, c, x, y] *)

tools.name: SpheroidalPS
tools.description: Angular spheroidal functions PS and QS (SpheroidalPS, SpheroidalQS), radial spheroidal functions S1/S2 (SpheroidalS1, SpheroidalS2) and SpheroidalEigenvalue: the separated solutions of the Helmholtz equation in prolate/oblate spheroidal coordinates, used for scattering by spheroids and band-limited signal analysis (prolate spheroidal wave functions).
tools.usage:
SpheroidalPS[n, m, gamma, z]
SpheroidalQS[n, m, gamma, z]
SpheroidalS1[n, m, gamma, z]
SpheroidalEigenvalue[n, m, gamma]
tools.example:
SpheroidalEigenvalue[2, 0, 1.5]
Plot[SpheroidalPS[2, 0, 1.5, x], {x, -1, 1}]

tools.name: ClebschGordan
tools.description: Clebsch-Gordan coefficients <j1 m1 j2 m2 | j m> for coupling angular momenta, with ThreeJSymbol, SixJSymbol and WignerD (Wigner rotation matrix elements D^j_{m1 m2}) covering the rest of quantum angular-momentum algebra.
tools.usage:
ClebschGordan[{j1, m1}, {j2, m2}, {j, m}]
ThreeJSymbol[{j1, m1}, {j2, m2}, {j3, m3}]
SixJSymbol[{j1, j2, j3}, {j4, j5, j6}]
WignerD[{j, m1, m2}, psi, theta, phi]

parameters.name: {j, m}
parameters.description: Angular momentum quantum numbers (integers or half-integers).

tools.name: HeavisideTheta
tools.description: Heaviside step function (undefined at 0, unlike UnitStep which is 1 there), the distributional partner of DiracDelta for symbolic integration, Laplace transforms and DSolve with switched inputs; HeavisidePi (unit pulse) and HeavisideLambda (unit triangle) are its box and hat relatives, and DiracComb the impulse train.
tools.usage:
HeavisideTheta[x]
HeavisidePi[x]
HeavisideLambda[x]
DiracComb[x]
tools.example:
D[HeavisideTheta[t - 2], t] (* DiracDelta[-2 + t] *)
LaplaceTransform[HeavisideTheta[t - a] f[t - a], t, s]
DSolve[{y'[t] + y[t] == HeavisideTheta[t - 1], y[0] == 0}, y, t]
tools.notes: Use UnitStep, UnitBox, UnitTriangle in purely numerical work; the Heaviside forms carry the generalized-function semantics.

tools.name: UnitBox
tools.description: UnitBox[x] is 1 for |x| < 1/2 and 0 otherwise, UnitTriangle[x] the unit hat function; together with UnitStep, Ramp, Clip and Boole they form the numeric piecewise building blocks for windowing, sampling and signal reconstruction formulas.
tools.usage:
UnitBox[x]
UnitTriangle[x]
UnitBox[x, y]
tools.example:
Plot[{UnitBox[x], UnitTriangle[x]}, {x, -2, 2}]
FourierTransform[UnitBox[t], t, w] (* Sinc-type result *)

tools.name: SquareWave
tools.description: Periodic waveforms with unit period: SquareWave (values -1/1, or custom {ymin, ymax}), TriangleWave and SawtoothWave. Use them as symbolic inputs to DSolve/NDSolve, for Fourier series demonstrations and as sources in signal-processing examples.
tools.usage:
SquareWave[x]
SquareWave[{ymin, ymax}, x]
TriangleWave[x]
SawtoothWave[x]
SawtoothWave[{ymin, ymax}, x]

parameters.name: {ymin, ymax}
parameters.description: Output range (default {-1, 1} for SquareWave, {0, 1} for SawtoothWave).

tools.example:
Plot[{SquareWave[t], TriangleWave[t], SawtoothWave[t]}, {t, 0, 3}]
FourierSeries[SquareWave[t], t, 5]
NDSolveValue[{x''[t] + x[t] == SquareWave[t/10], x[0] == 0, x'[0] == 0}, x, {t, 0, 50}]

tools.name: Sinc
tools.description: Sinc[x] = Sin[x]/x with Sinc[0] = 1 (unnormalized convention), the Fourier transform of a box and the kernel of Whittaker-Shannon interpolation. Listable and symbolically integrable; note the engineering sinc(pi x) convention differs by the factor Pi.
tools.usage: Sinc[x]
tools.example:
Integrate[Sinc[x], {x, -Infinity, Infinity}] (* Pi *)
reconstruct[t_] := Sum[samples[[k]] Sinc[Pi (t - k dt)/dt], {k, Length[samples]}]

tools.name: LogisticSigmoid
tools.description: The logistic sigmoid 1/(1 + Exp[-x]), Listable and differentiable; the standard activation in ElementwiseLayer, the inverse link of logistic regression and the CDF of the standard logistic distribution. Gudermannian and its inverse (InverseGudermannian) relate circular and hyperbolic functions in Mercator projections.
tools.usage:
LogisticSigmoid[x]
Gudermannian[x]
InverseGudermannian[x]
tools.example:
D[LogisticSigmoid[x], x] // Simplify (* LogisticSigmoid[x] (1 - LogisticSigmoid[x]) *)
ElementwiseLayer[LogisticSigmoid]
Gudermannian[Log[Tan[Pi/4 + phi/2]]] == phi // FullSimplify

tools.name: CubeRoot
tools.description: Real cube root of a real number (CubeRoot[-8] = -2), whereas (-8)^(1/3) gives the principal complex root; Surd[x, n] is the real n-th root for odd n. Use them whenever a real-valued root of a negative number is intended, e.g. in plotting and physical formulas.
tools.usage:
CubeRoot[x]
Surd[x, n]

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Root index (odd n allows negative x).

tools.name: Sec
tools.description: The remaining trigonometric and hyperbolic functions and inverses: Sec, Csc, Cot, Sech, Csch, Coth, ArcSec, ArcCsc, ArcCot, ArcSinh, ArcCosh, ArcSech, ArcCsch, ArcCoth. All are exact, arbitrary-precision, complex-analytic and understood by Integrate, Simplify and TrigExpand; ArcCosh and ArcSinh are the natural inverses in hyperbolic geometry and catenary/relativity formulas.
tools.usage:
Sec[z]
Csc[z]
Cot[z]
ArcSinh[z]
ArcCosh[z]
ArcCot[z]
Coth[z]
tools.example:
Integrate[Sec[x], x] (* -Log[Cos[x/2] - Sin[x/2]] + Log[Cos[x/2] + Sin[x/2]] *)
ArcCosh[2] // N
Simplify[Cot[x]^2 + 1 == Csc[x]^2]

tools.name: Haversine
tools.description: Haversine[z] = Sin[z/2]^2 and InverseHaversine, the functions of the haversine formula for great-circle distances; useful when implementing geodesic distance by hand (GeoDistance does it automatically with an ellipsoid model).
tools.usage:
Haversine[z]
InverseHaversine[z]
tools.example:
hav[{lat1_, lon1_}, {lat2_, lon2_}, r_] := 2 r ArcSin[Sqrt[Haversine[lat2 - lat1] + Cos[lat1] Cos[lat2] Haversine[lon2 - lon1]]]
hav[{40.7, -74.0} Degree, {51.5, -0.1} Degree, 6371.]

tools.name: FractionalD
tools.description: Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative/integral of order alpha, with CaputoD the Caputo fractional derivative used in initial-value problems; DSolve solves linear fractional ODEs with CaputoD in terms of MittagLefflerE. Available since 13.1.
tools.usage:
FractionalD[f, {x, alpha}]
FractionalD[f, {x, alpha}, x0]
CaputoD[f, {x, alpha}]
DSolve[CaputoD[y[t], {t, alpha}] == eqn, y[t], t]
tools.example:
FractionalD[x^2, {x, 1/2}] (* (8 x^(3/2))/(3 Sqrt[Pi]) *)
CaputoD[Sin[t], {t, 1/2}]
DSolve[{CaputoD[y[t], {t, 1/2}] == -y[t], y[0] == 1}, y[t], t]

tools.name: FactorialPower
tools.description: FactorialPower[x, n] is the falling factorial x (x-1) ... (x-n+1) (with a step form FactorialPower[x, n, h]), the polynomial basis of finite-difference calculus; it belongs to the gamma family alongside Pochhammer (rising factorial), Gamma[a, z] (upper incomplete gamma), Gamma[a, z0, z1], Beta[z, a, b] (incomplete beta) and PolyGamma[n, z]. Prefer the regularized forms (GammaRegularized, BetaRegularized) for numerically stable CDFs.
tools.usage:
FactorialPower[x, n]
FactorialPower[x, n, h]
Pochhammer[a, n]
Gamma[a, z]
Gamma[a, z0, z1]
Beta[z, a, b]
PolyGamma[n, z]

tools.name: QPochhammer
tools.description: q-analogues: QPochhammer (q-shifted factorial), QFactorial, QBinomial, QGamma, QPolyGamma and QHypergeometricPFQ, used in partition theory, quantum groups and combinatorics of Young diagrams; Sum recognizes q-series and returns them.
tools.usage:
QPochhammer[a, q]
QPochhammer[a, q, n]
QFactorial[n, q]
QBinomial[n, m, q]
QGamma[z, q]
QHypergeometricPFQ[{a1, ...}, {b1, ...}, q, z]
tools.example:
QPochhammer[q, q] (* Euler function: generating function of partitions inverse *)
Series[1/QPochhammer[q, q], {q, 0, 10}] (* PartitionsP coefficients *)
QBinomial[4, 2, q] // Expand
